content: 1. A lumbar puncture is recommended in cases where there is evidence of a bleeding disorder. This recommendation is strong, but the quality of evidence supporting it is very low. 2. Neuroimaging, such as ultrasound in young infants, CT, or MRI, should be considered for children presenting with altered consciousness or new focal neurological deficits. This recommendation is strong, but the quality of evidence is very low. 3. Pulse oximetry is recommended for detecting hypoxaemia in infants and children and for guiding oxygen therapy administration. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is low. 4. Pulse oximetry should be used wherever possible to detect hypoxaemia in children with severe lower respiratory infections, especially in those who are drowsy or lethargic. This is a strong recommendation, but the quality of evidence is low to very low. 5. Children with hypoxaemia should receive appropriate oxygen therapy. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is low. 6. Effective oxygen delivery systems should be a universal standard of care and made more widely available. This is a strong recommendation based on expert opinion. 7. The administration of oxygen therapy should be guided by pulse oximetry where available, and thresholds for oxygen delivery may vary depending on altitude. This is a strong recommendation, but the quality of evidence is very low. 8. Children living at altitudes ≤2500 meters above sea level should receive oxygen therapy if their oxygen saturation is ≤90%, as measured by pulse oximetry. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is very low. 9. For children living at high altitudes (>2500 meters above sea level), where normal oxygen saturation levels are lower, a threshold of SpO2 ≤87% may be used for initiating oxygen therapy. This is a recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 10. Nasal prongs are the preferred method for delivering oxygen to infants and children under five years of age with hypoxaemia requiring oxygen therapy. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 11. If nasal prongs are unavailable, nasal or nasopharyngeal catheters can be used as alternative delivery methods. Face masks or head-boxes are not recommended. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 12. Children with hypoxaemia should be closely monitored using pulse oximetry. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is very low. 13. Oxygen therapy should be discontinued when oxygen saturation remains stable above 90% (at ≤2500 meters above sea level) or 87% (at >2500 meters above sea level) for at least 15 minutes on room air in a clinically stable child. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is very low. 14. Pulse oximetry is recommended to detect hypoxaemia in all children with emergency signs as per ETAT (Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment). For children with only respiratory distress, oxygen supplementation is recommended at SpO2 <90%. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is very low. 15. Oxygen therapy can be stopped when the child no longer has ETAT emergency signs and maintains an oxygen saturation of SpO2 ≥90% in room air. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 16. For standard-flow oxygen therapy, humidification is not required. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is very low. 17. In emergency settings, if a flow of >4 L/min through nasal cannulae is required for more than 1–2 hours, effective heated humidification should be added. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is very low. 18. Children in shock with severe anaemia (haemoglobin <5 g/dL or haematocrit <15%) should receive a blood transfusion as early as possible and other IV fluids only to maintain normal hydration. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is low. 19. Children with severe acute malnutrition who are in shock should receive 10–15 mL/kg of IV fluids over the first hour. If they improve after the initial infusion, they should receive only oral or nasogastric maintenance fluids. If no improvement is seen after 1 hour, a blood transfusion (10 mL/kg slowly over at least 3 hours) should be given. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is low. 20. Analgesic treatment for persistent pain in children should follow a two-step approach based on the severity of pain. Paracetamol and ibuprofen should be available for the first step. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is low. 21. Strong opioid analgesics are recommended for the relief of moderate to severe persistent pain in children with medical illnesses. Morphine is the first-line strong opioid recommended for this purpose. There is insufficient evidence to recommend any alternative opioid over morphine. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is low. 22. Immediate-release oral morphine formulations should be available for treating persistent pain in children with medical illnesses. Child-appropriate prolonged-release oral dosage forms should also be available if affordable. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is low. 23. Switching opioids or routes of administration is strongly recommended in cases of inadequate analgesic effect or intolerable side effects. Alternative opioids and dosage forms should be available to practitioners, in addition to morphine, if possible. Routine rotation of opioids is not recommended. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is low. 24. Oral administration of opioids is the recommended route of administration. Alternative routes should be chosen based on clinical judgment, availability, feasibility, and patient preference when oral administration is not possible. Intramuscular administration should be avoided in children. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is very low. 25. A careful distinction should be made between end-of-dose pain episodes, incident pain related to movement or procedures, and breakthrough pain. Children with persistent pain should receive regular medication to control pain and appropriate medicines for breakthrough pain. This is a strong recommendation, though the quality of evidence is very low. 26. The use of corticosteroids as adjuvant medicines is not recommended for treating persistent pain in children with medical illnesses. This is a weak recommendation, with very low-quality evidence. 27. The use of bisphosphonates as adjuvant medicines is not recommended for treating bone pain in children. This is a weak recommendation, with very low-quality evidence. 28. For children exposed to intimate partner violence at home, psychotherapeutic interventions, including sessions with and without their mother, should be offered. However, the applicability of this recommendation in lowand middle-income settings is unclear. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-quality evidence. 29. For children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), family psycho-education should be provided. Parent skills training should be considered when available. Teachers should be contacted (with consent) to provide advice and plan for special educational needs. Anticipate major life changes and arrange personal and social support. Psychosocial interventions, such as cognitive behavioral therapy and social skills training, should be considered based on availability. Carers should be assessed for the impact of behavioral disorders and offered support for their personal, social, and mental health needs. Medicines should not be used for behavioral disorders in children and adolescents. 30. Healthcare providers should be alert to clinical features and risk factors associated with child maltreatment and assess for maltreatment without putting the child at increased risk. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence. 31. Psychological interventions, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT), may be offered for children and adolescents with emotional disorders. Caregiver skills training focused on their caregivers may also be offered. This is a conditional recommendation with low-quality evidence. 32. Non-specialized healthcare providers can support, collaborate, and facilitate referrals to and from community-based rehabilitation (CBR) programs for adults with developmental disorders, including intellectual disabilities and autism spectrum disorders, if available. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-quality evidence.
